explanations.answer: Everything the LORD did in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, opens with Egypt: “You have seen with your own eyes everything the LORD did in Egypt to Pharaoh, to all his officials, and to all his land.” These people are eyewitnesses. Nobody in that crowd can say they only heard it from a cousin. I like a sermon that starts with what you already know.

explanations.answer: The walls of Jericho falling down
explanations.explanation: Great story, friend, and it's real. The wall of Jericho does fall (Joshua 6:20). But Moses isn't pointing there. He starts with Egypt, with what the LORD did to Pharaoh, his officials and his land.

explanations.answer: The tower of Babel going up
explanations.explanation: The tower of Babel is a real story, but it's way back in Genesis 11:4-9. Moses isn't talking about that one. He's talking about what this crowd saw with their own eyes, and that's everything the LORD did in Egypt. I think you reached a little too far back on the shelf, baker.

Moses says it plainly: “Yet to this day the LORD has not given you a mind to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear.” That's a lot to say right after all those wonders. I think that stings a little to hear. It sure would sting me.

Good guess, since a whole lot of law comes up in this book. But the sentence lists a mind to understand, eyes to see and ears to hear. The law isn't what's missing in that verse. Moses is standing right there talking to them, so the word is mind.

Close to home, since Moses is the one leading them and he's standing right in front of them. But that's not the word in the verse. The LORD hasn't given them “a mind to understand, eyes to see, or ears to hear.” So the blank is mind.

Sandals lasting forty years sounds impossible, so I get the pause. But Moses says the opposite: “…your clothes and sandals did not wear out.” Forty years of desert walking and nothing wore through. My oven mitts give up after one rough season, so this one stays with me.

Right, they did not wear out. Moses says it right there: “…your clothes and sandals did not wear out.” That's forty years in the wilderness. My oven mitts can't make it through a single winter, so I'm still shaking my head.

explanations.answer: So they might know He is the LORD their God
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the verse gives. Moses says they ate no bread and drank no wine or strong drink, “…so that you might know that I am the LORD your God.” The text gives us the reason, so we don't have to guess at one. Simple and clear.

explanations.answer: So they would be strong enough for battle
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a reasonable guess, friend, but the verse never says it. The reason it gives is “…so that you might know that I am the LORD your God.” Battles do come up in this passage, but not as the reason for this. I'd stick with what the text says.

explanations.answer: So they would long for the promised land
explanations.explanation: It's a nice thought, but the text doesn't say that. The verse gives one reason: “…so that you might know that I am the LORD your God.” I'm not going to add one the Bible doesn't. That's like adding sprinkles to a recipe that never asked for them.

Yes. Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan came out against them in battle, “but we defeated them.” Two kings came out to fight, and Israel came out on top. Moses says it short and simple, so I will too.

Not this time, friend. Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan came out against them in battle, and Moses says, “but we defeated them.” Two kings showed up to fight and Israel won. I know it reads fast, so it's easy to blink and miss it.

That's the word. Moses says they took the land and “gave it as an inheritance” to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh. An inheritance is something handed down to be theirs, and I think that's a good word for it.

Tribute is a real word, but it's not the one here. The land was given “as an inheritance” to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh. Nobody was paying anyone in this verse. The land was given to them.

An outpost would be a little post at the edge of things. The verse says the land was given “as an inheritance” to the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh. That means it was theirs to keep, not a little spot to watch from. So the word is inheritance.

Yes, and Moses says it plainly: “So keep and follow the words of this covenant, that you may prosper in all you do.” That's the reason right there. I like a command that comes with its reason attached.

It's actually true, friend. Moses says, “So keep and follow the words of this covenant, that you may prosper in all you do.” The reason is right in the verse. Sometimes the plain reading is the whole answer.

They're actually in, friend. Verse 11 names “the foreigners in your camps who cut your wood and draw your water.” They're standing there with the leaders, the elders and the officials. Nobody is sent to the back.

Right, they are not left out. Moses lists them in the gathering: “the foreigners in your camps who cut your wood and draw your water.” They stand right alongside the leaders and elders. Everybody on that list is standing there.
That's it. The verse says the LORD will “…establish you today as His people…” and that He will be their God. It's a belonging word, and it fits beautifully. Nothing about swords or crowns in it.

I can see why that came to mind, with the kings and battles in the passage. But the verse says He will “…establish you today as His people…” It's not an army. It's a people, and the LORD is their God.
Big word, friend, but not the one in the verse. It says the LORD will “…establish you today as His people…” No empire is mentioned. He will be their God, and they will be His people.

explanations.answer: Those who are not here today
explanations.explanation: That's right. Moses says the covenant and the oath are also with “those who are not here today.” It reaches past the crowd in front of him. I think that's a big thing to hear if you were one of the people standing there.

The nations they passed through do come up later in Moses' sermon, but not here. In this verse the covenant is with those standing there “in the presence of the LORD our God, as well as with those who are not here today.” The text doesn't name the nations as part of it. So that one's a no.

explanations.answer: The people of the land of Moab
explanations.explanation: Moab is where they're standing, friend, and that's why it came to mind. But the verse doesn't name the people of Moab. It names those standing there and “those who are not here today.” Stick with what the verse says.

Yes. Moses says, “You saw the abominations and idols among them made of wood and stone, of silver and gold.” They'd passed through the nations and seen it with their own eyes. That's quite a shelf of idols.

It's actually true. Moses says, “You saw the abominations and idols among them made of wood and stone, of silver and gold.” Wood, stone, silver and gold, all of it made by hand. They passed those nations on the way here.

That's the one. Moses says, “Make sure there is no root among you that bears such poisonous and bitter fruit.” Nothing sweet about it. A bad root gives a bad harvest, and I'd rather not taste that one.
That's the opposite of what Moses says. The root bears “such poisonous and bitter fruit.” Nothing sweet about it, and nothing about plenty. I'm not eating that fruit, friend.
It's a tricky one, but the verse doesn't say small or hidden. It says the root “bears such poisonous and bitter fruit.” Poisonous and bitter is how Moses describes it. Not small, not hidden.

explanations.answer: Blot it out from under heaven
explanations.explanation: That's what Moses says. The LORD “…will blot out his name from under heaven…” It's a heavy thing to read, and I think it's meant to be. Moses says it so they'll take the warning seriously.

explanations.answer: Keep it among the tribes forever
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Moses says. The LORD “…will blot out his name from under heaven…” A name kept forever is a happy ending. This one isn't. It's a heavy part, so we'll take it slowly.

explanations.answer: Carve it on the city gate
explanations.explanation: Interesting guess, but there's no city gate in this verse. Moses says the LORD “…will blot out his name from under heaven…” It's a heavy line, and the text has no gate in it. So we stay with what the verse says.

explanations.answer: A burning waste of sulfur and salt
explanations.explanation: That's what Moses says: “All its soil will be a burning waste of sulfur and salt, unsown and unproductive, with no plant growing on it.” It's a hard picture. I've burned a batch before, but nothing close to that.

explanations.answer: A muddy swamp full of reeds
explanations.explanation: A swamp is pretty far from this picture. Moses says the soil will be “a burning waste of sulfur and salt,” with “no plant growing on it.” Reeds are plants, so they wouldn't fit. Burning and salty is the picture.

Thornbushes are plants, and the verse says there will be “no plant growing on it.” Moses describes the soil as “a burning waste of sulfur and salt.” So it's not a forest, friend. It's a bare, burning waste.
Yes. The destruction is “just like the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in His fierce anger.” Moses names four places. It's a sobering comparison.

It's actually true. Moses says the land will be “just like the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, which the LORD overthrew in His fierce anger.” Sodom and Gomorrah are right there in the verse, with two more places named alongside them. It's a heavy comparison.

That's the word. The people will answer, “It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers…” They walked away from it. This is why Moses says to make sure no heart turns away.

Renewing is what Moses is doing in Moab today, so I see why it came to mind. But in the answer the nations hear, the people “abandoned the covenant of the LORD.” They walked away from it. The blank is abandoned.

Sealed sounds like a covenant word, but it's not in this verse. The answer says, “It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers…” They left it behind. The word is abandoned.
The text says the opposite. They “worshiped gods they had not known—gods that the LORD had not given to them.” So those gods weren't from the LORD at all. It's an easy one to flip.
Right, they were not. They worshiped “gods they had not known—gods that the LORD had not given to them.” The LORD gave them no such gods. That line is plain and clear.

explanations.answer: Uprooted them and cast them into another land
explanations.explanation: That's what the answer says: “The LORD uprooted them from their land in His anger, rage, and great wrath, and He cast them into another land, where they are today.” It's a heavy verse. I think it hurts to read, so we'll go gently.

explanations.answer: Left them in the land to serve their enemies
explanations.explanation: That's not what this verse says. The answer says the LORD “uprooted them from their land” and “cast them into another land.” They aren't left in the land. It's a heavy verse, so I'll just stay with what it says.

explanations.answer: Gave their land to the foreigners living there
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say that. It says the LORD “uprooted them from their land in His anger, rage, and great wrath, and He cast them into another land, where they are today.” The people are the ones cast out. It's a heavy part, and we'll stay close to the text.
That's right. Moses says, “…the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever…” He says us, so he's counting himself in. What the LORD has revealed is theirs to hold onto.
The verse doesn't narrow it down like that. Moses says the revealed things belong “to us and to our children forever.” There's no 'alone' in that line. It's for all of them and their children.

The nations around them come up in this passage, but not in this verse. Moses says the revealed things belong “to us and to our children forever.” That's Moses and the people standing there, plus their children. The nations aren't named.
That's the word. The revealed things are theirs “…so that we may follow all the words of this law.” They aren't given just to know. They're given to follow.
Proclaiming sounds loud and good, friend, and that's why it came to mind. But the verse says the revealed things are theirs “…so that we may follow all the words of this law.” The word is follow.

Memorizing is a fine habit, but it's not the word here. The verse says “…so that we may follow all the words of this law.” Knowing it is one thing, and following it is what the verse asks. The word is follow.
